Voice Control is not Siri. Siri takes a request and decides what to do about it. Voice Control takes a command and performs it, exactly, on whatever is in front of you. It is a mouse and a keyboard made of words. Apple shipped it in twenty nineteen, in macOS Catalina and iOS thirteen, and the recognition runs on the device itself. After the one time download, it works with the network switched off.

Everything Voice Control does rests on one idea. Before you can act on a thing, the thing needs a name. So there are three ways to give it one, and you climb down them only as far as you need. First, the label it already has. Say, tap Send. Second, a number. Say, show numbers, and every control on screen puts one on. Then say, tap fourteen. Third, the grid. Say, show grid, and the screen is cut into numbered squares. Say a number, and that square becomes a grid of its own. Two or three steps in, you are pointing at a single pixel of a photo, inside an app that never labelled anything.

Inside a text field, what you say becomes text, and the editing commands keep working. Select the previous word. Replace going tomorrow with going to Denver. Capitalize that. Say, correct that, and a list of alternatives appears. The hard part is telling text and commands apart, and Voice Control settles it in one direction. A phrase it recognises as a command is a command. If a particular one keeps getting in your way, you can switch that single command off and leave the rest alone.

A touchscreen expects fingers. Voice Control supplies them. Swipe, scroll, long press, zoom and rotate are all commands, and they compose with the grid, so a gesture can begin at square nineteen and end wherever you say. Every hardware button has a phrase too. Go home. Lock screen. Open Control Center.

Two settings do most of the personal work. Custom commands bind a phrase you choose to an action, a shortcut, or a run of keystrokes. Vocabulary teaches it the words it would otherwise fight you on. Names, jargon, the spelling your team uses. And when you need it to stop listening, say, go to sleep. After that it listens for one phrase only. Wake up.

Voice Control was built for people who cannot use a touchscreen or a trackpad, and it is held to that standard. Every part of the interface has to be reachable by voice alone. That is why the grid exists, and why the overlay can be left on screen permanently. On an iPhone with Face ID, it can stop listening the moment you look away. Your audio stays on the device unless you opt in to send it to Apple. What you are left with is an operating system you can drive with a sentence.
Replace going tomorrow with going to Denver.
